Fun game, but UI needs work. The default button for each room is to leave the room instead of interacting with the room. And there is too much clicking needed for this process - it can definitely be streamlined. Also, the buttons don't stand out enough clearly against the background - it's difficult to see what is interactive. And some weird text choices, like what is "BGM"? Oh, that's music, so why not just label the control "Music" then? Finally, the battles really need a pause button, and possibly a log of events, so you can look back and see why you are winning or losing. The start of the game is tedious. Continuously clicking on rooms, on icon, on button, on card, on accept card, on back to dungeon. Why not just start the game with 3 card choices? The shuffle reward mechanic is another waste of time. Rather just give the player a random card instead of making them click three times and watch a pointless animation. There is no scrollbar on the map, so you can't go back to previous rooms. Finally, the fade to black and back to the screen transition whenever entering and exiting a room gets tiresome. It's not stylish, it just wastes time.

Villages & Dungeons is a surprisingly engaging indie strategy title that combines roguelike progression, deckbuilding systems, and autobattler mechanics into a compact but highly addictive experience. Developed by CaCaFrog Studio and published by Morax Games, the game focuses less on flashy presentation and more on rewarding experimentation and tactical planning. At first glance it may resemble many other pixel-art card battlers currently available on Steam, but after a few runs it becomes clear that Villages & Dungeons has enough unique ideas to stand apart from the crowd. The game succeeds by turning simple mechanics into something consistently satisfying through clever build creation and strategic decision-making. The basic structure revolves around exploring randomized dungeons while building a combat setup capable of surviving increasingly dangerous encounters. Unlike traditional deckbuilders that overwhelm players with huge card collections during battles, Villages & Dungeons keeps its combat system focused through a smaller but more deliberate setup mechanic. Players combine a primary combat card with several support cards, creating synergies that dramatically affect performance during automatic battles. This system may sound restrictive at first, but it actually encourages thoughtful experimentation because every choice carries weight. Even small adjustments to a build can completely change how encounters play out. One of the strongest aspects of the game is how rewarding it feels to discover effective combinations between cards, elements, and upgrades. Different elemental themes such as fire, water, light, dark, and nature interact in interesting ways, allowing players to create builds focused on poison damage, explosive attacks, healing loops, defensive sustain, or rapid combo chains. The game constantly pushes players to adapt based on what cards and relics appear during a run. Sometimes a weak early setup unexpectedly evolves into a devastating strategy capable of destroying entire waves of enemies with minimal effort. That sense of experimentation becomes the core reason the game remains addictive over time. Combat itself plays out automatically once encounters begin, placing emphasis entirely on preparation and strategy rather than direct control. This autobattler approach will not appeal to everyone, especially players who prefer active turn-based combat, but Villages & Dungeons handles the concept well because battles are fast and easy to read. Watching carefully planned builds either succeed brilliantly or fail disastrously creates a unique tension throughout each dungeon run. The game almost feels like solving a constantly evolving puzzle where victory depends on understanding interactions and timing rather than reflexes. The roguelike structure also contributes heavily to the game’s replay value. Dungeons are randomized, events alter progression paths, and every run introduces different opportunities or setbacks. Permanent upgrades earned between runs provide a satisfying sense of long-term progression without making the game feel overly dependent on grinding. Failed runs rarely feel pointless because players continue unlocking new possibilities and learning stronger strategies. The constant cycle of experimentation, failure, and gradual mastery keeps the gameplay loop engaging for far longer than expected. Another impressive feature is the depth hidden beneath the game’s relatively simple presentation. There are numerous cards, runes, upgrades, and fusion mechanics that allow players to customize strategies in meaningful ways. Some builds focus entirely on overwhelming offense while others rely on survival, attrition, or status effects. Discovering overpowered combinations becomes one of the most enjoyable parts of the experience. The game rewards creativity, and players willing to test unusual setups often uncover surprisingly effective strategies that completely transform how they approach future runs. Visually, Villages & Dungeons adopts a retro-inspired pixel-art style that prioritizes clarity over spectacle. Character sprites, enemies, and menus are functional and easy to understand even during busy encounters. While the environments and effects may not reach the artistic quality of larger indie roguelikes, the clean presentation works well enough for the game’s strategic focus. The interface occasionally feels cluttered when managing multiple systems at once, but overall the visuals remain readable and accessible. The soundtrack is decent and fits the fantasy atmosphere without becoming especially memorable. Music mostly exists to support the dungeon-crawling experience rather than dominate it, providing calm background themes during exploration and more energetic tracks during combat. Sound effects effectively communicate attacks, abilities, and enemy actions, though audio presentation is clearly secondary to the gameplay systems themselves. Despite its strengths, Villages & Dungeons is not flawless. Some players may struggle to connect with the autobattler format because direct interaction during fights is limited. Once battles begin, success largely depends on preparation rather than active decision-making. Certain builds can also feel noticeably stronger than others, occasionally reducing strategic variety once dominant combinations are discovered. Balance adjustments and additional content updates could help maintain freshness during longer play sessions. The game’s production values are another area where its indie budget becomes obvious. Animations are fairly basic, menus sometimes feel rough around the edges, and the overall presentation lacks the polish of larger strategy titles. Technical issues and interface frustrations occasionally interrupt the flow as well, particularly for newer players trying to understand the game’s many overlapping systems. However, most of these issues become easier to overlook once the core gameplay loop starts revealing its depth. What ultimately makes Villages & Dungeons enjoyable is how well it captures the excitement of building increasingly powerful strategies through experimentation. Every run feels like an opportunity to test new ideas, optimize synergies, and push unusual combinations to their limits. The game respects player creativity and provides enough mechanical depth to keep strategic players invested for dozens of hours. Even when runs fail, there is usually a sense that a better build or smarter decision could completely change the outcome next time. Villages & Dungeons may not have the visual polish or mainstream attention of bigger roguelike deckbuilders, but it delivers a surprisingly deep and rewarding strategy experience for players willing to invest time into its systems. Its combination of roguelike progression, deckbuilding mechanics, and autobattler combat creates a gameplay loop that is easy to revisit repeatedly. Fans of tactical experimentation and build-focused strategy games will likely find themselves hooked far longer than expected. Rating: 8/10

[code] [url=https://store.steampowered.com/curator/36948155-Card-Game-KING/] FOR MORE CARD AND BOARD GAMES FOLLOW US [b]CARD GAME KING [/b][/url] [/code] Villages and Dungeons is an elaborate rock paper scissor roguelike game where you build an autobattling engine using a creature and only 4 support cards. Its simple looks can be deceiving as there is quite a bit of skill involved in building the right engine and managing the dungeon pathing. On top of those, the resource management is well done too, where meta progression resources can be used to "revive" and retry battles, leading to interesting decision on whether to "go all in" or accept the loss and gear up for the next attempt. It's an addicting gameplay loop, albeit a bit grindy at times as you are nudged into battles just to scrap together some resources or open up new paths. It does have a few other frustrating elements to it. There is a bit of RNG to both the battles and card drafting. This means you may lose battles or get stuck in front of an unbeatable opponent because you didn't get offered the right cards. Example is encountering an opponent with high defense but no cards that could reliably puncture those. There are no consumables either that can get you out of a tight spot so once you hit a wall, it's sometimes unscalable. Whats worse, on top of already stripped down UI, after each battle you are greeted with the mobile leftover popups such as dev requesting you to give the game a high rating. Every. Single. Time. I feel like the game could've been better if it had gotten a few more passes to smooth over some rough edges, but as it is now, it's equal parts addicting and frustrating. [h1][b]Favorite mechanics[/b][/h1] • Interesting revival system that uses meta progression resources [h1][b]The positive[/b] [/h1] + Surprisingly tactical + Fair amount of ways to build your engine [h1][b]The neutral[/b][/h1] * There is no option to view enemy cards without re-entering battles * Annoying occasional mobile leftover pop ups [h1][b]The negative[/b][/h1] - No logs or pause button makes all the action a bit overwhelming at times - Promotes grind - Luck can be a deciding factor at times [h1][b]Conclusion:[/b] [/h1] An elaborate rock-paper-scissors autobattler with card drafting that's addicting to play, but poor UI, luck dependency and grind bring it down a notch. Recommended, 7/10.
